backup.info: OpenIPC U-Boot overwrites the original crypto partition making it impossible to revert to the factory firmware unless you have a full flash backup for this particular camera! To create a full firmware backup start a TFTP server and run these commands in bootloader shell.
backup.more_info_html: Please refer to Installation instructions in the project's wiki for more information.
backup.shared_name: The name above is the same for every camera of this model and chip, so backing up a second one writes over the first — and this file is the only way back to a camera's stock firmware. Give each camera's backup a name of its own, and use that same name when restoring it. Or fill in the MAC address above: when the form has one, it becomes part of the name.

installation.compound_caveat_html: If your bootloader answers with a usage message instead of running the line, it does not understand &&. The line is three commands — the transfer, the erase, then the write — and all three have to be entered, each one only after the part before it has reported success; that check is what && does for you. Do not leave the erase out: a write onto flash that was not erased first stores garbage, reports success anyway, and at offset 0 that garbage is the bootloader.

flashing_full.info: The full firmware image consists of bootloader, kernel and root filesystem, and is also suitable for flashing memory chip using a programmer. Please note, the full image does not contain pre-set environment, so the IP addresses and other settings are yours to add. The MAC address is not one of them — the camera assigns itself a stable unique address on first boot and keeps it.
flashing_full.mac_note_html: The full image carries no environment, so this is where the address you entered above goes. You only need it to keep an address the camera already has — the one on its own label. Left empty, the camera picks a stable unique address for itself on first boot and keeps it, so there is nothing to set here and nothing will ask you for one later. If the bootloader answers Can't overwrite "ethaddr", an address is already set and there is nothing to do here.
flashing_full.nand_caveat: On NAND the image covers the bootloader, kernel and UBI root filesystem only, not the whole chip, and it is not suitable for a programmer -- it carries no OOB/ECC bytes and no factory bad-block markers. Write it from U-Boot, or use the per-partition commands below.

installation.lock_caveat_html: sf lock 0 clears the block protection some vendors arm in the flash chip's status register, and it is OpenIPC U-Boot's own subcommand: a stock bootloader built from mainline U-Boot has sf protect and no lock, so it answers with the sf usage message instead. Nothing was changed by that, and on most chips nothing is armed — enter the rest of the block exactly as written and it flashes normally. Where sf protect does exist it is worth one try, with the same offset and length as the sf erase below, but most chips answer that it is unsupported. What is lost either way is a check: flash that is still protected discards an erase and a write while reporting success, so a camera that comes back on its stock firmware after every command said OK is what that looks like. That bootloader cannot clear the protection — flash the chip with an external programmer, or with defib over the serial console you are already on, whose flash agent unlocks it itself.
installation.mac_record_caveat_html: Write this address down with the backup. The full image erases the whole chip and the factory MAC goes with it: on first boot the camera keeps an address it already has, then looks for the factory one still in flash, and mints itself a new one only when it finds neither — and after a whole-chip erase there is nothing left to find. If the bootloader answers that ethaddr is not defined, the address is on the camera's own label. Either way you can give it back afterwards with set_mac aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff on the camera.
installation.mac_record_stock_caveat_html: Write this address down with the backup. The factory MAC lives in flash, so anything that erases the chip takes it with it: on first boot the camera keeps an address it already has, then looks for the factory one still in flash, and mints itself a new one only when it finds neither. If the bootloader answers that ethaddr is not defined, the address is on the camera's own label. Either way you can give it back afterwards with set_mac aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff on the camera.

installation.stock_backup_info: You are about to write over the firmware the camera shipped with, and without a copy of it there is no way back. Start a TFTP server and run these commands in your camera’s bootloader shell — they use nothing the bootloader already on the board does not have.
installation.stock_bundle_info_html: Unpack it into the root directory of your TFTP server. Inside are {kernel}, the kernel, and {rootfs}, the root filesystem.
installation.stock_info_html: This site cannot print these two commands. Where the kernel and the root filesystem go depends on the partition layout your camera's bootloader was built with, and that differs between cameras carrying the same chip — OpenIPC's own offsets arrive with OpenIPC's bootloader, which this SoC does not have. Read your layout with printenv bootargs and printenv mtdparts, then the installation guide walks through writing the two files. If it does not cover your camera, ask in the chat — this is the step people help each other with.
installation.stock_lede: OpenIPC publishes firmware for this SoC but not a bootloader for it, so the guided installation and the ready-made flash image — both of which begin by writing an OpenIPC bootloader — are not offered here. What you can do is install this firmware from the bootloader your camera already has, and the first step of that is the same on every camera.

success.info_html: Open camera's web interface on http://{address}/. A new camera has no password yet and streams nothing until it has one, so it asks you to choose a password before anything else. That password belongs to root and is the one the web interface, ssh, UART and RTSP all use. ONVIF accepts it too, unless your client authenticates with a digest -- those need onvif.password set separately.
